title: Keeping Unfit Drugs from Patients: Returns, Return to Stock, Adulteration and Misbranding, Recalls, Drug Samples and Cold Storage
topic: Product integrity / Returned medication, recalls, drug samples and refrigerated storage
subtopic: Accepting, quarantining and not reusing medication returned by patients under 247 CMR 9.01(7), read with 9.01(5) and the 9.16(1) records; returning prepared but undispensed prescriptions to stock under 247 CMR 9.13, with the 9.19(5) stock-container label; adulteration and misbranding under 21 U.S.C. 351 and 352, the prohibited acts in 21 U.S.C. 331 and the dispensed-label treatment in 21 U.S.C. 353(b); recalls under 21 CFR part 7 and 247 CMR 9.19(12); drug samples under 21 U.S.C. 353(c) and (d), 21 CFR part 203 and 247 CMR 9.01(6); and refrigerated and frozen storage under 247 CMR 9.22 and Board Policy 2020-05
learning_objectives: Sort a patient's returned medication into the mandatory and discretionary limbs of 247 CMR 9.01(7) and state what happens to any medication the pharmacy accepts.
Explain why 247 CMR 9.01(5) keeps a voluntarily accepted return out of re-dispensing, and give the safe course where 247 CMR 9.01(7)'s quarantine sentence is arguable.
Use the 247 CMR 2.00 definition of dispensing to decide whether a filled prescription may be returned to stock under 247 CMR 9.13.
State the container, label, policy and recall conditions of 247 CMR 9.13, and explain why a lot number belongs on a returned-to-stock label although 9.13 does not list it.
Distinguish the adulteration grounds of 21 U.S.C. 351 from the misbranding grounds of 21 U.S.C. 352 and apply the prohibited acts in 21 U.S.C. 331(c) and (k) to stock held for sale.
State what 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2) requires on a dispensed prescription label and which misbranding grounds survive the exemption.
Read a recall notice by class and by depth under 21 CFR part 7, present part 7 as guidance, and apply the binding Massachusetts duty in 247 CMR 9.19(12).
Identify who may lawfully receive prescription drug samples, why a retail pharmacy may not, and what 247 CMR 9.01(6) adds.
Apply 247 CMR 9.22 and Board Policy 2020-05 to cold-storage equipment, monitoring, excursions and records.

orientation.text: This section is about the points at which a drug that should not reach a patient can still reach one, and about which body of law closes each of them. Four of the controls are Massachusetts regulations addressed to the pharmacy or the licensee and bind as written: the acceptance and quarantine of medication a patient brings back under 247 CMR 9.01(7), the return to stock of a prescription that was prepared but never dispensed under 247 CMR 9.13, the duty to effectuate a recall under 247 CMR 9.19(12), and the equipment, monitoring and records for refrigerated and frozen medication under 247 CMR 9.22. The federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act supplies the statutory vocabulary of adulteration and misbranding in 21 U.S.C. 351 and 352, the prohibited acts in 21 U.S.C. 331, and the ban on selling, purchasing or trading drug samples in 21 U.S.C. 353(c). Two layers are not regulation in the ordinary binding sense and are taught as what they are: 21 CFR 7.40 through 7.59, which FDA itself frames as guidance on recalls, and Board Policy 2020-05, to which 247 CMR 9.22(3) points for temperatures. Where a federal and a Massachusetts provision both reach the same act, the pharmacy complies with both, which in practice means the stricter one governs.

247 CMR 9.01(7) sorts medication a patient brings back by why it came back. A pharmacy shall accept a medication that it previously dispensed to a patient if the medication was dispensed to the patient in error, or is suspected to be defective or contaminated. A pharmacy is not required to accept a medication from a patient that was properly dispensed and not defective at the time it was dispensed, so a change of therapy or an unwanted surplus creates no duty to take the medication back. The two mandatory limbs are independent: suspected contamination triggers the duty even where the original dispensing was entirely correct. Acceptance is not reuse. A medication accepted by a pharmacy pursuant to 247 CMR 9.01 may not be returned to the pharmacy's inventory and must be quarantined and properly disposed, and the paragraph states no exception to that sentence, for an unopened container, an intact seal or a pharmacist's inspection. The disposal leaves a record: under 247 CMR 9.16(1) a pharmacist and pharmacy keep purchasing and return records and disposal and destruction records in a readily retrievable manner for at least two years.

Two provisions from neighbouring subjects frame that duty. The first is 247 CMR 9.01(5): unless otherwise permitted by law, regulation, or Board policy, a licensee may not re-dispense any medication which has been previously dispensed. Its words turn on the medication's having been dispensed, not on how or why it came back, so a pharmacy that chooses to take back a properly dispensed medication it was not required to accept still may not re-dispense it unless a law, regulation or Board policy permits that. Whether the quarantine-and-dispose sentence of 247 CMR 9.01(7) also reaches such a voluntary acceptance is arguable, because the sentence speaks of a medication accepted pursuant to 247 CMR 9.01 without distinguishing the two kinds; the course that is safe on either reading is to keep it out of inventory, quarantine it and dispose of it properly. The second is that some returns carry law of their own that is taught elsewhere: a returned controlled substance, whose security while quarantined and whose destruction or transfer belong with controlled-substance security and disposal; a patient's unwanted medication taken back for disposal, which belongs with take-back; the provision 247 CMR 9.08 makes for compliance packaging, taught with dispensing automation and packaging; and the report and analysis a dispensing error triggers, taught with quality-related events.

247 CMR 9.13 governs a different situation, and the word that separates it from a return is dispensed. 247 CMR 2.00 defines dispensing as the physical act of delivering a drug to an ultimate user pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner, including the packaging and labeling necessary to prepare it for delivery. A prescription that was filled and labeled but never picked up, or that went out for delivery and came back undelivered, was prepared for dispensing but not dispensed. For that medication 247 CMR 9.13(1) says the pharmacy may return it to stock, which is a permission and not a duty, and if the pharmacy does so it shall ensure that the medication is not returned to the manufacturer's stock bottle and that it is kept in the original patient container or placed in an appropriate container with a label affixed showing the product name, the strength or concentration, the name of the manufacturer, supplier, or NDC number, and the expiration date assigned at the time of filling. 247 CMR 9.13(2) requires a policy and procedure regarding returning medications to stock. The regulation states no time limit within which the return must happen, and it does not require a new expiration date: the date on the label is the one assigned when the prescription was filled.

The label list in 247 CMR 9.13(1)(b) does not include a lot number, and 247 CMR 9.13(3) shows why that matters. In the event of a recall, a pharmacy may not dispense any medication that has been returned to stock and is potentially subject to the recall unless it can confirm the specific lot number is not included in the recall. A returned-to-stock container whose lot cannot be traced is therefore unusable for the life of any recall of that product. Separately, 247 CMR 9.19(5) requires a pharmacy to store medications in the manufacturer's stock bottles or in other stock containers clearly labeled with the product name, strength or concentration, NDC number, manufacturer or supplier, lot number, assigned expiration date, and the date the medication was transferred out of its original stock bottle. Whether that general storage label also governs a returned-to-stock container, or whether the specific list in 247 CMR 9.13 displaces it, the regulations do not say. The course that is safe on either reading is to label a returned-to-stock container with every element of both lists, which also leaves the pharmacy able to make the lot confirmation 247 CMR 9.13(3) demands. Returning to stock is itself taught here; the verification of the original fill and any automation or compliance packaging it passed through belong to their own subjects.

Federal law describes an unfit drug in two statutory categories. Adulteration, in 21 U.S.C. 351, concerns the drug itself and the conditions around it: among other grounds, a drug consisting in whole or in part of a filthy, putrid or decomposed substance; a drug prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have been contaminated with filth or rendered injurious to health; a drug whose manufacture, processing, packing, or holding does not conform to current good manufacturing practice; a drug whose strength differs from, or whose quality or purity falls below, its compendial standard or what it purports to possess; and a drug with which another substance has been mixed to reduce its quality or strength or for which one has been substituted. Misbranding, in 21 U.S.C. 352, concerns labeling and packaging: among other grounds, labeling that is false or misleading in any particular, a package without the name and place of business of the manufacturer, packer, or distributor and an accurate quantity statement, labeling without adequate directions for use and adequate warnings, a misleading container, an imitation of another drug, or a drug offered for sale under the name of another drug. Neither section, in the grounds read for this section, names expiration as a ground. That does not make expired stock usable: 247 CMR 9.01(12), taught with the conduct standards, forbids dispensing or distributing expired, outdated, defective, contaminated or otherwise substandard drugs to a person or entity not licensed or legally authorized to receive them, and the safe course taught there is that such product is not dispensed to a patient.

The categories reach a pharmacy through the prohibited acts in 21 U.S.C. 331. Paragraph (c) prohibits the receipt in interstate commerce of an adulterated or misbranded drug and the delivery or proffered delivery of it for pay or otherwise. Paragraph (k) is the one written for stock on a shelf: it prohibits the alteration, mutilation, destruction, obliteration, or removal of the whole or any part of a drug's labeling, or the doing of any other act with respect to the drug, if the act is done while the drug is held for sale, whether or not the first sale, after shipment in interstate commerce, and results in the drug being adulterated or misbranded. Holding stock under insanitary conditions whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health, or covering its labeling with a false statement, can be acts of that kind when they produce that result. The dispensed prescription has its own treatment. Under 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(1), dispensing a prescription drug other than on a valid written, oral or authorized refill prescription is deemed an act which results in the drug being misbranded while held for sale. Under 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2), a drug dispensed on a practitioner's prescription is exempt from section 352 if its label carries the name and address of the dispenser, the serial number and date of the prescription or of its filling, the name of the prescriber, the name of the patient if stated in the prescription, and the directions for use and cautionary statements, if any, contained in the prescription. The exemption is not total: false or misleading labeling under 352(a), the imitation and other-name grounds in 352(i)(2) and (3), and the packaging requirements of 352(g), (h) and (p) still apply, and the exemption is lost for a drug dispensed in violation of 353(b)(1) or in a business of dispensing on diagnosis by mail. Massachusetts label content for the dispensed container is taught with the dispensing label.

A drug recall is the firm's action, and FDA oversees it: FDA's own recall page says a recall may be recommended or requested by FDA or initiated voluntarily at any time by a company, and that FDA's role is to oversee the company's recall strategy. 21 CFR 7.40 describes recall as a voluntary action and says that 7.40 through 7.59 provide guidance so that responsible firms may discharge their recall responsibilities; a recall may be undertaken by a manufacturer or distributor on its own initiative or at FDA's request. Under 21 CFR 7.3(g) a recall is a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that FDA considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which it would initiate legal action; a market withdrawal, involving a minor violation not subject to legal action or no violation, and a stock recovery, involving product that has not left the firm's direct control, are not recalls. FDA assigns the classification under 7.3(m) by relative degree of health hazard: Class I where there is a reasonable probability that use of or exposure to the product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death, Class II where use or exposure may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or the probability of serious consequences is remote, and Class III where use or exposure is not likely to cause adverse health consequences. The classification is not the reach of the recall. Depth is a separate element of the recall strategy under 7.42(b)(1): the consumer or user level, the retail level, or the wholesale level. A retail-level recall stops at the pharmacy shelf; only a consumer or user level recall extends to patients.

A pharmacy usually meets a recall as a consignee, anyone who received, purchased, or used the product. Under 21 CFR 7.49 the recalling firm is responsible for promptly notifying each affected direct account, and its communication conveys that the product is subject to a recall, that further distribution or use of remaining product should cease immediately, where appropriate that the account should notify its own customers, and what to do with the product, identifying the product by size, lot numbers, codes or serial numbers. 7.49(d) says consignees that receive a recall communication should immediately carry out the recalling firm's instructions and, where necessary, extend the recall to their consignees. That is federal guidance and is worded as should. The Massachusetts layer is a mandate: 247 CMR 9.19(12) provides that a pharmacy shall effectuate a recall of medication that is or may be defective in any way. The paragraph does not define a recall or list the steps, and it is arguable whether it reaches only recalls a firm has begun or also requires the pharmacy to act on its own when it learns that medication may be defective. On either reading the safe course is the same: take the identified lots out of dispensing, carry out the recalling firm's instructions to the depth the communication states, withhold returned-to-stock medication whose lot cannot be confirmed as outside the recall, and act on medication that may be defective even before a defect is confirmed. The texts do not turn every recall into an instruction that every patient stop therapy; patient-level action follows the depth and instructions of the particular recall. The return of recalled controlled substances to a supplier under 21 CFR 1317.10, and the quarantine of commingled lots in pharmacy processing automation under 247 CMR 9.11, are taught with their own subjects.

Drug samples are the clearest case of product that is fit but may not be sold. 21 U.S.C. 353(c)(1) provides that no person may sell, purchase, or trade or offer to sell, purchase, or trade any drug sample, defined as a unit of a prescription drug which is not intended to be sold and is intended to promote the sale of the drug, and 21 U.S.C. 331(t) makes a sale, purchase or trade in violation of 353(c) a prohibited act. Distribution is closed as tightly. Under 21 U.S.C. 353(d) and 21 CFR 203.30 and 203.31, a manufacturer or authorized distributor of record may distribute samples, by mail or common carrier or through a representative, only to practitioners licensed to prescribe the drug or, at the written request of a licensed practitioner, to the pharmacy of a hospital or other health care entity, on a written request received before delivery and a receipt signed on delivery. 21 CFR 203.3 defines a health care entity to exclude any retail pharmacy, so a community pharmacy is not a lawful recipient at all. Providing a sample to a patient by the prescriber, by a health care professional acting at the prescriber's direction and under supervision, or by a hospital or health care entity pharmacy acting at a prescriber's direction that received the sample lawfully, is not a distribution. Each sample unit is labeled to show its status, for example sample, not for sale, or professional courtesy package. Massachusetts adds 247 CMR 9.01(6): a licensee may not accept or purchase medications designated as drug samples not for resale for the purpose of compounding, repacking, or in any way reselling them, so the bar reaches a sample handed over free as much as one bought. 247 CMR 2.00 defines a drug sample as a unit of a prescription drug that is not intended to be sold. What a prescriber may dispense from office samples of a controlled substance in Massachusetts is taught with the special rules for controlled-substance prescriptions.

247 CMR 9.22 turns cold storage into checkable conditions. A pharmacy shall maintain policies and procedures ensuring that proper refrigeration equipment is available, of adequate size, and used to maintain proper refrigerator and freezer temperatures, and those policies and procedures shall include a protocol to respond to any out of range temperature, including an assessment of the integrity of the medication. The pharmacy shall use a combination refrigerator/freezer, a standalone refrigerator or a standalone freezer; freezer units shall be frost-free with an automatic defrost cycle unless otherwise approved by the Board; and a pharmacy may not use an appliance that contains a freezer compartment within the refrigerator space, such as a dorm-style refrigerator, however well it holds temperature. It shall measure and maintain temperatures in accordance with Board guidance, maintain temperature logs that clearly identify out of range temperatures, document the actions taken in response, and keep those records for at least one year. It may not store any food or beverage in a refrigerator or freezer used to store medications. The regulation itself states no temperature range and no checking frequency; those come from the Board guidance it points to.

That guidance is Board Policy 2020-05, Refrigerated and Frozen Medication Storage. Citing USP <1079>, it sets the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and the freezer at -13°F to 14°F (-25°C to -10°C). It calls for temperatures of each unit to be reviewed and documented at least twice daily, for a mechanism to identify excursions on any day the pharmacy is closed, for each log to identify the unit and the reviewer and to be readily retrievable, for calibrated thermometers with a certificate of calibration testing, and for a back-up plan for a power failure. Its excursion action plan includes documenting the excursion, assessing its length and magnitude and quarantining products as necessary, contacting manufacturers to confirm safety and efficacy, removing from active inventory any visibly altered or damaged product, such as refrigerated product that has been frozen, and any product the manufacturer cannot confirm safe and effective, documenting that confirmation before product returns to active inventory, and notifying the patient and the patient's health care provider if unsafe or ineffective product was dispensed or administered. The policy also says that for highly temperature sensitive medications a freezer without an automatic defrost cycle may be used with a manual defrosting process. The current regulation instead requires frost-free units unless otherwise approved by the Board, and whether the policy's statement is itself that approval is arguable; the safe course is a frost-free unit unless the pharmacy has confirmed the Board's approval for the unit it proposes. Maintaining the cold chain in delivery and shipping is taught with medication supplied outside the counter, and storage of compounded preparations and hazardous drugs with compounding operations.

worked_examples.scenario: On one afternoon a Massachusetts pharmacy handles three items. A patient returns an unopened bottle of tablets she was given in the wrong strength. Another returns a correctly dispensed, non-defective inhaler because his prescriber changed therapy, and asks for a refund. A third patient's filled and labeled prescription has sat unclaimed in the pick-up area for three weeks. A technician proposes restocking all three.
steps: Sort the first item under 247 CMR 9.01(7). It was dispensed in error, so the pharmacy shall accept it. Once accepted it may not be returned to inventory and must be quarantined and properly disposed; the unopened bottle changes nothing.

Sort the second. It was properly dispensed and not defective when dispensed, so the pharmacy is not required to accept it. If the pharmacy chooses to take it, 247 CMR 9.01(5) still bars re-dispensing a previously dispensed medication unless law, regulation or Board policy permits, and the safe course is quarantine and proper disposal.

Sort the third under 247 CMR 9.13. Dispensing is the physical act of delivery to the ultimate user, and this medication was never delivered, so it was prepared but not dispensed and may be returned to stock.

Apply the conditions to the third. Not into the manufacturer's stock bottle; keep it in the original patient container or an appropriate container with a label showing product name, strength or concentration, manufacturer, supplier or NDC number, and the expiration date assigned at filling, under the pharmacy's return-to-stock policy and procedure. Three weeks is not a bar, because 9.13 sets no time limit, and adding the lot number keeps the container usable during a recall.
Record the disposition. Return and disposal records for the first two items are kept readily retrievable for at least two years under 247 CMR 9.16(1).
worked_examples.resolution: Only the unclaimed prescription may go back to stock, and only on the 247 CMR 9.13 conditions. The error the scenario invites is treating all three as one kind of return, when a medication that was dispensed may not re-enter inventory while one that was never dispensed may.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy receives a Class II recall communication from its wholesaler naming two lots of a blood-pressure tablet at the retail level. The shelf holds a stock bottle from one named lot, a stock bottle from an unnamed lot, and two returned-to-stock prescription vials whose labels show product, strength, NDC and expiration date but no lot number. A pharmacist proposes calling every patient on the drug and telling them to stop taking it.
steps: Read the classification and the depth separately. Class II describes the hazard under 21 CFR 7.3(m); the retail depth under 7.42(b)(1) takes the recall to the pharmacy's stock, not to product already dispensed.

Act on the communication. Under 21 CFR 7.49(d) a consignee should immediately carry out the recalling firm's instructions, and under 247 CMR 9.19(12) the pharmacy shall effectuate a recall of medication that is or may be defective, so the named lot comes out of dispensing and is handled as the instructions direct.
Leave the unnamed lot alone unless the instructions say otherwise; the communication identifies product by lot so that unaffected stock can stay in use.

Test the two returned-to-stock vials under 247 CMR 9.13(3). They are potentially subject to the recall and the pharmacy cannot confirm that their specific lot number is not included, so they may not be dispensed.

Answer the pharmacist. Nothing in part 7 or 247 CMR 9.19(12) makes every recall an instruction for all patients to stop therapy; a retail-level recall does not extend to patients, and a consumer-level recall would carry its own instructions.
worked_examples.resolution: Pull the named lot and the two untraceable returned-to-stock vials, keep dispensing from the unnamed lot, and do not tell every patient to stop. The error the scenario invites is reading the class as the depth, or treating an untraceable returned-to-stock vial as safe because the stock bottle beside it is from an unaffected lot.

worked_examples.scenario: A drug representative, turned away by a nearby clinic, offers a Massachusetts community pharmacy a carton of sealed prescription drug samples labeled not for sale, free of charge. The manager suggests dispensing them on paid prescriptions, and a staff pharmacist suggests instead repacking them into vials and giving them away at cost. A hospital pharmacy across town receives the same product under a prescriber's written request.
steps: Identify the product. Each unit is labeled to show its sample status, and a drug sample under 21 U.S.C. 353(c)(1) is a unit of a prescription drug not intended to be sold and intended to promote its sale.

Test the community pharmacy as a recipient. Under 21 U.S.C. 353(d) and 21 CFR 203.30 and 203.31 samples go only to practitioners licensed to prescribe or, on a practitioner's written request, to the pharmacy of a hospital or other health care entity, and 21 CFR 203.3 excludes any retail pharmacy from health care entity.
Test the manager's plan. Dispensing on paid prescriptions is a sale of drug samples, forbidden to any person by 353(c)(1) and a prohibited act under 21 U.S.C. 331(t).

Test the pharmacist's plan under 247 CMR 9.01(6). A licensee may not accept or purchase drug samples not for resale for the purpose of repacking or in any way reselling them, and accepting them free does not take the plan outside the bar.

Place the hospital pharmacy. On a licensed practitioner's written request it is a lawful recipient, and providing a sample to a patient at a practitioner's direction is not a distribution; it still may not sell the samples or accept them to repack or resell.
worked_examples.resolution: The community pharmacy declines the carton outright; neither plan is lawful. The error the scenario invites is thinking that a free, sealed sample or a sale at cost escapes the ban, when the federal channel excludes retail pharmacies and both laws forbid resale.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacist opens the pharmacy on a Monday and finds the medication refrigerator reading 58°F after a weekend power cut. It holds unopened insulin glargine pens and vaccines. The unit is a standalone refrigerator. A technician resets the breaker, watches the reading fall back to 40°F within an hour, and proposes moving on because the unit is back in range.
steps: Recognise the excursion. Board Policy 2020-05, to which 247 CMR 9.22(3) points, sets the refrigerator range at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C), so 58°F is out of range, and the policy expects a mechanism to identify excursions on days the pharmacy is closed.

Apply the regulation. 247 CMR 9.22(1) requires the protocol to include an assessment of the integrity of the medication, and 247 CMR 9.22(4) requires the log to show the out of range temperature and the actions taken, kept for at least one year.
Follow the Board's action plan. Document the excursion, assess its length and magnitude, quarantine product as necessary, and contact the manufacturers to confirm safety and efficacy.

Decide disposition. Product the manufacturer cannot confirm safe and effective, and any visibly altered product, comes out of active inventory; product that is confirmed returns only after the confirmation is documented.
Check what already left. If unsafe or ineffective product was dispensed or administered, the policy calls for notifying the patient and the patient's health care provider.
worked_examples.resolution: The pens and vaccines are quarantined and assessed, not released because the unit recovered. The error the scenario invites is treating a return to range as proof of integrity, when the regulation requires an integrity assessment and documented response.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy's stock is shipped to it by an out-of-state wholesaler. To clear space, a technician transfers loose tablets from a nearly empty manufacturer's bottle into a clean amber vial labeled only with the drug name and strength, and covers a damaged manufacturer's label with a hand-written sticker giving a different strength from the one inside. Later a pharmacist dispenses from both containers, and one dispensed label omits the prescriber's name.
steps: Test the storage container under 247 CMR 9.19(5). A stock container other than the manufacturer's bottle must be clearly labeled with product name, strength or concentration, NDC number, manufacturer or supplier, lot number, assigned expiration date and the transfer date; two elements are not enough.

Test the covered label under 21 U.S.C. 352(a) and 331(k). Labeling showing a strength other than the contents is false or misleading in any particular, and altering labeling while the drug is held for sale after interstate shipment, with that result, is a prohibited act.
Test the dispensed container under 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2). The exemption from section 352 requires the prescriber's name on the label, so that container does not qualify.
Note what the exemption would never have covered. Even a fully labeled dispensed container remains subject to 352(a), so a strength misstatement carried onto a dispensed label is still misbranding.
worked_examples.resolution: Both stock containers must be corrected or removed from use, and the dispensed label must carry the federal elements. The error the scenario invites is assuming that the prescription label exemption shields a pharmacy from every misbranding ground once a drug is dispensed.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.01(7), which two situations oblige a pharmacy to accept a medication it previously dispensed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: When the medication was dispensed to the patient in error, or is suspected to be defective or contaminated.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Must a pharmacy accept a properly dispensed, non-defective medication a patient no longer wants?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 247 CMR 9.01(7) states that a pharmacy is not required to accept a medication that was properly dispensed and not defective at the time it was dispensed.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a returned medication accepted under 247 CMR 9.01(7) may go back into inventory if its seal is intact.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. A medication accepted pursuant to 247 CMR 9.01 may not be returned to the pharmacy's inventory and must be quarantined and properly disposed; the paragraph states no exception for an intact container.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why is a filled prescription that was never picked up eligible for return to stock under 247 CMR 9.13?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because it was prepared for dispensing but not dispensed; 247 CMR 2.00 defines dispensing as the physical act of delivering the drug to an ultimate user.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the four elements of the return-to-stock label in 247 CMR 9.13(1)(b).
retrieval_prompts.answer: Product name; strength or concentration; name of the manufacturer, supplier, or NDC number; and the expiration date assigned at the time of filling.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long does a pharmacy have to return an unclaimed prescription to stock under 247 CMR 9.13?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.13 states no time limit; it conditions how the medication is returned, not when.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: During a recall, when may a pharmacy dispense returned-to-stock medication that is potentially subject to it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Only if it can confirm that the specific lot number is not included in the recall (247 CMR 9.13(3)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 9.19(12) require of a pharmacy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That it effectuate a recall of medication that is or may be defective in any way.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Match the recall classes: serious adverse health consequences or death reasonably probable; temporary or medically reversible consequences; not likely to cause adverse consequences.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Class I; Class II; Class III (21 CFR 7.3(m)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What are the three depths of recall a recall strategy may specify under 21 CFR 7.42(b)(1)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The consumer or user level, the retail level, and the wholesale level.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Are a market withdrawal and a stock recovery recalls under 21 CFR 7.3?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. A recall under 7.3(g) does not include a market withdrawal or a stock recovery.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How does 21 CFR 7.49(d) word a consignee's response to a recall communication?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Consignees should immediately carry out the instructions set forth by the recalling firm and, where necessary, extend the recall to their consignees; it is guidance, whereas 247 CMR 9.19(12) is a Massachusetts mandate.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 U.S.C. 331(k), when does an act done to a drug on the shelf become a prohibited act?
retrieval_prompts.answer: When it is done while the drug is held for sale, whether or not the first sale, after shipment in interstate commerce, and results in the drug being adulterated or misbranded.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A drug held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have been contaminated: adulterated or misbranded?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Adulterated, under 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(A).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which parts of 21 U.S.C. 352 still apply to a drug dispensed on a prescription whose label meets 353(b)(2)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Paragraph (a), paragraphs (i)(2) and (3), and the packaging requirements of (g), (h) and (p); (k) and (l) are also named but have been repealed.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must the label of a dispensed prescription carry for the 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2) exemption?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The name and address of the dispenser, the serial number and date of the prescription or of its filling, the name of the prescriber, the name of the patient if stated in the prescription, and the directions for use and cautionary statements, if any, contained in the prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: May a retail pharmacy lawfully receive prescription drug samples from a manufacturer's representative?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Samples go to licensed practitioners or, on a practitioner's written request, to the pharmacy of a hospital or other health care entity, and 21 CFR 203.3 excludes any retail pharmacy from health care entity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.01(6), which acts and which purposes are forbidden with drug samples not for resale?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Accepting or purchasing them, for the purpose of compounding, repacking, or in any way reselling them.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What refrigerator and freezer ranges does Board Policy 2020-05 set?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Refrigerator 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C); freezer -13°F to 14°F (-25°C to -10°C).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long must refrigerator and freezer temperature records be kept under 247 CMR 9.22(4)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least one year.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a dorm-style refrigerator is acceptable if a continuous logger shows it stays in range.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 247 CMR 9.22(2) forbids an appliance with a freezer compartment within the refrigerator space, such as a dorm-style refrigerator, whatever its temperatures.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long are return records and disposal and destruction records kept under 247 CMR 9.16(1)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: At least two years, in a readily retrievable manner.

quick_review.text: 247 CMR 9.01(7): a pharmacy shall accept a medication it previously dispensed if it was dispensed in error or is suspected defective or contaminated, and is not required to accept one properly dispensed and not defective when dispensed.
A medication accepted pursuant to 247 CMR 9.01 may not be returned to inventory and must be quarantined and properly disposed.
247 CMR 9.01(5) bars re-dispensing any previously dispensed medication unless law, regulation, or Board policy permits it.
Return to stock under 247 CMR 9.13 is for medication prepared for dispensing but not dispensed, and is a permission rather than a duty.

Returned-to-stock medication never goes into the manufacturer's stock bottle; it stays in the original patient container or an appropriate container labeled with product name, strength or concentration, manufacturer, supplier or NDC number, and the expiration date assigned at filling.
247 CMR 9.13 requires a policy and procedure for returning medications to stock and states no time limit.
During a recall, returned-to-stock medication potentially subject to it is not dispensed unless the specific lot number is confirmed not included.

247 CMR 9.19(5) stock containers other than the manufacturer's bottle carry product name, strength or concentration, NDC, manufacturer or supplier, lot number, assigned expiration date and transfer date.
247 CMR 9.19(12): a pharmacy shall effectuate a recall of medication that is or may be defective in any way.
21 CFR 7.40 through 7.59 are guidance; recall is a voluntary action by the firm, on its own initiative or at FDA's request.

Class I: serious adverse health consequences or death reasonably probable. Class II: temporary or medically reversible consequences, or serious consequences remote. Class III: not likely to cause adverse consequences.
Depth of recall is consumer or user, retail, or wholesale, and is separate from class.
Adulteration (21 U.S.C. 351) concerns the drug and how it was prepared, packed or held; misbranding (21 U.S.C. 352) concerns labeling and packaging.
21 U.S.C. 331(c) and (k) reach receipt and delivery of adulterated or misbranded drugs and acts done while a drug is held for sale after interstate shipment.
21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2) exempts a properly labeled dispensed prescription from section 352 except (a), (i)(2) and (3), and the packaging requirements of (g), (h) and (p).
No person may sell, purchase, or trade a drug sample; samples go only to licensed practitioners or, on written request, to hospital or health care entity pharmacies, never to a retail pharmacy.
247 CMR 9.01(6): a licensee may not accept or purchase drug samples not for resale to compound, repack or resell them.

247 CMR 9.22: permitted refrigerator and freezer configurations, frost-free freezers unless the Board approves otherwise, no dorm-style units, an excursion protocol with an integrity assessment, logs, documented actions, one-year records, and no food or beverage.
Board Policy 2020-05: refrigerator 2°C to 8°C, freezer -25°C to -10°C, review and document each unit at least twice daily.

decision_logic.condition: A patient brings back a medication the pharmacy dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Ask why. If it was dispensed in error or is suspected defective or contaminated, accept it. If it was properly dispensed and not defective when dispensed, acceptance is not required.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy has accepted a returned medication.
decision_logic.action: Keep it out of inventory, quarantine it and dispose of it properly, whatever the state of the container; do not re-dispense it unless a law, regulation or Board policy permits; keep the return and disposal records for at least two years.

decision_logic.condition: A filled prescription was never delivered to the patient.
decision_logic.action: It was not dispensed. It may be returned to stock if it does not go into the manufacturer's stock bottle, is kept in the original patient container or an appropriate container labeled with the 247 CMR 9.13 elements, and the pharmacy follows its return-to-stock policy and procedure; add the lot number so recall confirmation is possible.

Read the class (hazard) and the depth (how far down the chain) separately, carry out the recalling firm's instructions immediately, and effectuate the recall of medication that is or may be defective.

decision_logic.condition: Returned-to-stock medication might belong to a recalled lot.
decision_logic.action: Do not dispense it unless the pharmacy can confirm the specific lot number is not included in the recall.

decision_logic.condition: Stock may have been held in conditions that could have contaminated it or rendered it injurious to health.
decision_logic.action: Recognise that holding under insanitary conditions whereby a drug may have been contaminated or rendered injurious to health is adulteration under 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(A), and take the safe course of keeping it from sale until its status is resolved.

decision_logic.condition: Labeling on a drug held for sale is altered, covered or removed.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether the act results in adulteration or misbranding; if so it is a prohibited act under 21 U.S.C. 331(k), and false or misleading labeling is misbranding under 352(a).

decision_logic.condition: A dispensed prescription label is being checked against federal law.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the dispenser's name and address, prescription serial number and date, prescriber's name, patient's name if on the prescription, and directions and cautions; remember 352(a) and (i)(2)-(3) still apply.

decision_logic.condition: Someone offers the pharmacy prescription drug samples.
decision_logic.action: A retail pharmacy declines: it is not a lawful recipient, no person may buy, sell or trade samples, and a licensee may not accept samples not for resale to compound, repack or resell. A hospital or health care entity pharmacy may receive them only on a licensed practitioner's written request.

decision_logic.condition: A refrigerator or freezer reads out of range.
decision_logic.action: Log it, assess the integrity of the medication under the pharmacy's protocol, quarantine as necessary, confirm safety with manufacturers, remove unconfirmed or visibly altered product, document the actions and the confirmation, and notify patient and provider if unsafe product reached a patient.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy is choosing cold-storage equipment.
decision_logic.action: Use a combination refrigerator/freezer, standalone refrigerator or standalone freezer; no freezer compartment inside the refrigerator space; frost-free freezers with automatic defrost unless the Board has approved otherwise.

ma_vs_federal.text: Recalls: 21 CFR 7.49(d) says a consignee should carry out the recalling firm's instructions, which is guidance; 247 CMR 9.19(12) says a Massachusetts pharmacy shall effectuate a recall of medication that is or may be defective, which binds.

Samples: federal law bars any person from selling, purchasing or trading samples and limits who may receive them; 247 CMR 9.01(6) adds a Massachusetts bar on a licensee accepting or purchasing samples not for resale to compound, repack or resell them. A pharmacy satisfies both by not acquiring samples for any of those purposes.

Unfit product: federal adulteration and misbranding provisions define the categories and the prohibited acts; Massachusetts adds operational duties on returns, return to stock, stock labeling and cold storage that apply whether or not a drug is adulterated or misbranded.

Temperature: no federal provision read for this section fixes pharmacy refrigerator ranges; in Massachusetts 247 CMR 9.22(3) requires temperatures to be measured and maintained in accordance with Board guidance, and Board Policy 2020-05 supplies the ranges.
Dispensed label: 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2) states the federal elements for the exemption from section 352; Massachusetts label content is a separate requirement, and a pharmacy meets both.

exceptions.text: A pharmacy is not required to accept a medication that was properly dispensed and not defective at the time it was dispensed.
247 CMR 9.01(5) yields where law, regulation, or Board policy otherwise permits re-dispensing a previously dispensed medication.
Returned-to-stock medication potentially subject to a recall may be dispensed if the pharmacy confirms that the specific lot number is not included.

Freezer units must be frost-free with an automatic defrost cycle unless otherwise approved by the Board; Board Policy 2020-05 describes non-auto-defrost freezers for highly temperature sensitive medications with manual defrosting.
The 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2) label exemption does not apply to a drug dispensed in violation of 353(b)(1) or in a business of dispensing drugs pursuant to diagnosis by mail.

Providing a sample to a patient by a licensed practitioner, by a health care professional at the practitioner's direction and under supervision, or by a hospital or health care entity pharmacy acting at a practitioner's direction that lawfully received it, is not a distribution under 21 U.S.C. 353(d)(1).

timing_deadlines.event: Returning a prepared but undispensed prescription to stock
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No time limit is stated in 247 CMR 9.13
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy may return it whenever the 9.13 conditions are met; the label carries the expiration date assigned at filling.

timing_deadlines.event: Keeping return records and disposal and destruction records
timing_deadlines.consequence: Records are maintained in a readily retrievable manner under 247 CMR 9.16(1).

timing_deadlines.event: Keeping refrigerator and freezer temperature records
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.22(4) requires the records, including documented actions taken on out of range temperatures.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least twice daily for each unit, with a mechanism for days the pharmacy is closed
timing_deadlines.consequence: Board Policy 2020-05 item VIII; excursions that are not caught cannot be assessed.

timing_deadlines.event: Consignee response to a recall communication
timing_deadlines.consequence: 21 CFR 7.49(d) guidance says consignees should immediately carry out the recalling firm's instructions.

timing_deadlines.event: Recalling firm's notice to its direct accounts
timing_deadlines.consequence: 21 CFR 7.49(a) makes the recalling firm responsible for promptly notifying each affected direct account.

timing_deadlines.event: Returning excursion-affected product to active inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Only after confirmation of safety and effectiveness is documented
timing_deadlines.consequence: Board Policy 2020-05 item XV; product that cannot be confirmed is removed from active inventory.

forms_records.text: Return-to-stock label: product name; strength or concentration; name of the manufacturer, supplier, or NDC number; expiration date assigned at the time of filling (247 CMR 9.13(1)(b)).
A written policy and procedure regarding returning medications to stock (247 CMR 9.13(2)).

Stock container label for anything outside the manufacturer's stock bottle: product name, strength or concentration, NDC number, manufacturer or supplier, lot number, assigned expiration date and date transferred out of the original stock bottle (247 CMR 9.19(5)).
Purchasing and return records and disposal and destruction records, readily retrievable for at least two years (247 CMR 9.16(1)).
Cold-storage policies and procedures covering equipment, and a protocol to respond to any out of range temperature that includes an assessment of the integrity of the medication (247 CMR 9.22(1)).
Temperature logs that clearly identify out of range temperatures, documentation of the actions taken in response, and retention for at least one year (247 CMR 9.22(4)).

Under Board Policy 2020-05, each temperature log identifies the unit and the reviewer and is readily retrievable; excursion records show value, duration and time of day; confirmation of safety and effectiveness is documented before product returns to active inventory; equipment maintenance, monitoring and cleaning policy and a back-up plan are in place; thermometers carry a certificate of calibration testing.

Federal dispensed-prescription label: dispenser's name and address, serial number and date of the prescription or its filling, prescriber's name, patient's name if stated in the prescription, and directions for use and cautionary statements, if any (21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2)).

Drug sample paperwork runs through the manufacturer or authorized distributor of record: a licensed practitioner's written request before delivery and a receipt signed by the recipient on delivery and returned (21 CFR 203.30 and 203.31).

A recall communication identifies the product, size, lot numbers, codes or serial numbers, the reason and hazard, and specific instructions, with a ready means for the recipient to report whether it holds the product (21 CFR 7.49(c)).

role_duties.duty: Accept a previously dispensed medication returned because of a dispensing error or a suspected defect or contamination; keep any accepted return out of inventory, quarantine it and dispose of it properly.

If it returns undispensed medication to stock, keep it out of the manufacturer's stock bottle, label its container with the 247 CMR 9.13 elements, maintain a return-to-stock policy and procedure, and withhold it during a recall unless its lot is confirmed not included.
Store medications in manufacturer's stock bottles or fully labeled stock containers, and effectuate a recall of medication that is or may be defective.
Maintain purchasing and return records and disposal and destruction records, readily retrievable, for at least two years.

Maintain cold-storage policies and equipment meeting 247 CMR 9.22, measure and maintain temperatures under Board guidance, log and respond to excursions with an integrity assessment, keep records for a year, and keep food and beverage out of medication units.
Re-dispense no previously dispensed medication unless law, regulation, or Board policy permits, and accept or purchase no drug samples not for resale to compound, repack or resell them.

role_duties.role: Any person, including a pharmacy and its staff
role_duties.duty: Sell, purchase or trade no drug sample; receive in interstate commerce and deliver no adulterated or misbranded drug; do no act to a drug held for sale after interstate shipment that results in adulteration or misbranding.
Dispense prescription drugs only on a valid prescription or authorized refill, with a label carrying the federal elements of 21 U.S.C. 353(b)(2).
Develop the recall strategy, including depth, and promptly notify each affected direct account with a communication identifying the product and giving instructions.
Under 21 CFR 7.49(d) guidance, immediately carry out the recalling firm's instructions and, where necessary, extend the recall to its own consignees.

role_duties.role: Manufacturer or authorized distributor of record
role_duties.duty: Distribute samples only to licensed practitioners or, on a licensed practitioner's written request, to a hospital or health care entity pharmacy, against a written request and a signed receipt.
Issue the guidance under which temperatures are measured and maintained, and approve any freezer that is not frost-free with an automatic defrost cycle.

common_traps.text: Restocking a returned medication because its container is unopened. Once accepted under 247 CMR 9.01, it may not return to inventory.
Treating every patient return as mandatory, or every one as refusable. Only error and suspected defect or contamination compel acceptance.
Reading suspected contamination as needing a dispensing error too. Either limb alone triggers the duty to accept.
Treating an unclaimed filled prescription as previously dispensed. Dispensing is delivery to the ultimate user, so it may be returned to stock under 247 CMR 9.13.
Pouring returned-to-stock tablets back into the manufacturer's stock bottle because they never left the pharmacy.
Inventing a time limit for return to stock. 247 CMR 9.13 states none.
Assigning a fresh expiration date to returned-to-stock medication. The label carries the date assigned at the time of filling.
Dispensing an untraceable returned-to-stock vial during a recall because the lot on the shelf is unaffected. Without confirming the vial's own lot, it may not be dispensed.
Reading a recall's class as its depth. Class describes hazard; depth decides whether patients are reached.
Treating every recall as an instruction for all patients to stop therapy. Patient-level action follows the depth and instructions of the particular recall.
Treating 21 CFR part 7 as the only recall law in Massachusetts. 247 CMR 9.19(12) requires the pharmacy to effectuate a recall of medication that is or may be defective.

Calling expired stock adulterated or misbranded as a matter of course. The grounds in 21 U.S.C. 351 and 352 read for this section do not name expiration; the bar on dispensing expired product comes from 247 CMR 9.01(12).
Assuming the prescription label exemption removes every misbranding ground. False or misleading labeling, imitation and other-name grounds, and the named packaging requirements still apply.
Thinking free samples may be accepted by a retail pharmacy. A retail pharmacy is not a lawful recipient, and 247 CMR 9.01(6) bars accepting as well as purchasing samples to resell.
Accepting a dorm-style refrigerator because it holds temperature. The appliance itself is prohibited.
Returning excursion-affected product to use once the unit is back in range, without an integrity assessment and documented confirmation.
Presenting the refrigerator and freezer ranges as regulation text. They come from Board Policy 2020-05, to which 247 CMR 9.22(3) points.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Unopened insulin glargine held in a refrigerator that went out of range is not released because the unit recovers; the pharmacy assesses integrity, confirms safety with the manufacturer, documents the result and removes unconfirmed or visibly altered product from active inventory.
